results.title: Get transparency and predictability with the Azure Virtual Machine lifecycle
results.author: The Microsoft Azure Team
highlights:
Azure General Purpose, Memory Optimized, Compute Optimized, and Storage Optimized VMs are the first VM families covered by this policy.

The lifecycle stages, spanning Current, Extended, End of Life, and Retired, are defined below, with dedicated Microsoft investment levels, regional and quota availability, applicable purchasing options, and pricing. The policy establishes clear lifecycle stages, expected customer experiences, and Microsoft’s commitments at each stage so customers can confidently plan, deploy, and modernize workloads over time.

| Azure Virtual Machine Lifecycle Policy | |
| --- | --- |
| Stage | Description |
| Current | Customer recommendation: Customers can confidently deploy new workloads, expand existing deployments, and optimize their Azure investments using VMs in the Current stage of the lifecycle. These VMs are specifically recommended for new deployments. Microsoft investment: During this stage, products receive standard maintenance and support. Availability: Current VM series are generally available to customers and have broad availability across Azure regions globally. Purchasing options and pricing: Pay-as-you-go pricing and Azure Savings Plans. Azure Reserved VM Instances may also be offered. |
| Extended | Customer recommendation: Azure VMs in the Extended stage remain supported for existing workloads; however, customers should begin evaluating and planning a transition to VMs in the Current stage. Microsoft investment: During this stage, products continue to receive standard maintenance and support. Availability: VMs in the Extended stage remain generally available across multiple regions. However, VMs in this stage may be subject to quota restrictions. Purchasing options and pricing: Pay-as-you-go pricing and Azure Savings Plans. Azure Reserved VM Instances may also be offered. Changes to purchasing options and pricing are possible. |
| End of Life | Customer recommendation: VMs enter the End of Life stage when their retirement is formally announced. These VMs are based on older platform generations and do not benefit from the latest advancements in performance, security, reliability, and efficiency. Customers should actively plan and transition the workloads to VMs in the Current or Extended stages. Microsoft investment: During this stage, products continue to receive standard maintenance and support. In addition, Azure will provide notifications, migration tooling, and guidance to help customers move to newer versions. Availability: VMs in the End of Life stage remain available to existing customers in currently supported regions and within their existing quota allocations, subject to available capacity. New deployments and quota requests are subject to restriction. Microsoft will deploy new workload placement capabilities for VMs in the End of Life stage. While customers may experience minor workload performance variations in rare scenarios, existing Azure Virtual Machines SLAs will be met. These capabilities allow Microsoft to improve capacity availability for VMs in the End of Life stage as well as help support continued investments in modern hardware, new capabilities, and global scale. Purchasing options and pricing: Pay-as-you-go pricing and Azure Savings Plans remain available, while Reserved Instances may no longer be offered. When VMs enter the End of Life stage, customers should expect changes to pricing and availability. |
| Retired | Customer recommendation: Retired VMs are no longer available and can no longer be provisioned. Customer modernization should be complete, with workloads now deployed to VMs in the Current or Extended stages. Microsoft investment: VMs in a Retired series are no longer covered by a service level agreement (SLA) and are not eligible for Microsoft support. Availability: New VM creation is no longer available, and existing VMs will be deallocated. Purchasing options and pricing: VMs in a retired series are no longer available for purchase. |

results.title: Virtual Machine Retirement and Pricing Changes: Clarification Needed - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
## Problem description

I am seeking information about whether any of our current Windows virtual machines are scheduled to be retired in 2029 or if their prices will increase in 2027. I received an email about Azure VM series retirements and price changes and want to understand how it affects my resources.

...

2026-09-30T07:14:01.07+00:00 

I think the 2029 date depends on the VM series. For Azure public cloud, DCsv3/DCdsv3 retire on Oct 31, 2029, while Dv3/Dsv3/Ev3/Esv3 retire on Nov 15, 2029. The current VM SKU would help narrow down which retirement applies. The 2027 pricing change can’t be identified without the original notice. Could you share the VM SKU and the notice?

...

The impact depends on the specific VM series and reservation type. Microsoft has announced retirement schedules for certain older VM series, while pricing changes can also depend on reservation eligibility and expiration dates.

Recommended: 

Check Azure Advisor → Service Retirement and your VM sizes in the Azure portal to identify affected resources. For pricing, compare the current VM SKUs and reservations using the Azure Pricing Calculator.

Without the VM names/sizes (SKUs) and the original notification details, it isn't possible to confirm whether your specific Windows VMs are affected.

results.title: Azure GPU quota increase rejected due to insufficient payment history on new Pay-As-You-Go subscription - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
# Azure GPU quota increase rejected due to insufficient payment history on new Pay-As-You-Go subscription

 Amr Ezzat 25 Reputation points 

 2026-09-13T21:52:47.7833333+00:00 

Hi everyone,

I recently upgraded my Azure Free Trial subscription to Pay-As-You-Go because I want to deploy a GPU VM

I’m trying to deploy:

- VM:`Standard_NC4as_T4_v3`
- GPU: NVIDIA Tesla T4 16 GB
- Region: East US
- Required quota: 4 vCPUs
- Quota family:`Standard NCASv3_T4 Family vCPUs`

The problem is that my quota is currently 0, so I cannot deploy the VM.

I submitted a quota increase request, but Microsoft Support rejected it with this message:

> “Due to insufficient payment history, a previous bank decline, or an unpaid outstanding balance, Microsoft is currently unable to approve additional quota at this time.”

However, my billing account currently shows:

- Amount due: $0.00
- No payment needed
- Pre-tax total: $0.00
- I have no outstanding balance.
- I have also added a new payment method that supports international online payments and set it as my primary payment method.

This is a new Azure subscription, so I understand that I may not have much payment history yet.

...

Hi Amr Ezzat & thx for join me at Q&A platform,

This is most likely an account risk/eligibility restriction, not a normal quota-capacity issue. quota value of 0 for Standard NCASv3_T4 Family vCPUs on a newly converted Pay-As-You-Go subscription can happen when GPU families are restricted until the subscription has enough billing and trust history. The rejection text is fairly explicit that Microsoft’s internal risk checks are blocking the increase. A $0.00 balance and a valid payment method don’t necessarily satisfy those checks.

There isn’t a published minimum number of successful payments or a documented spend threshold that guarantees GPU quota approval. The decision is made by Microsoft’s internal quota/risk systems, so repeatedly submitting the same request usually won’t help if the subscription is still considered too new. I also wouldn’t expect switching from NC4as_T4_v3 to another GPU family to reliably bypass this. New subscriptions can have zero quota across several GPU families, and some series have even tighter availability controls.

The practical options are to keep the subscription in good standing and build some billing history, or reply to the existing quota support case and ask for a manual review, explaining that you only need 4 vCPUs for a single T4 VM and that the payment method has been corrected. If Microsoft confirms the restriction is based on account history, there isn’t a customer-side setting that can override it.

highlights:

The actual credit amount only shows up under the billing account that’s linked to that Founders Hub subscription. Azure Portal → Cost Management and Billing → that billing account → Azure credits.

results.title: Azure Sponsorship GPU quota request for NCASv3_T4 fails with QuotaNotAvailableForResource - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
Welcome to Microsoft Q&A,

Azure Sponsorship subscriptions are billing-classified as benefit subscriptions, and GPU VM families (NC, ND, NV series, including NCASv3_T4) are excluded from self-service quota increases on that subscription type by design. That's why the request succeeds at submission but fails during processing with `QuotaNotAvailableForResource`, and why it reproduces the same way in both East US and East US 2 (it's a subscription-level restriction, not a regional capacity issue).

#1 - Sponsorship/benefit subscriptions are excluded from GPU family quota allocation regardless of region.

#2 - Yes. If this subscription came from Microsoft for Startups Founders Hub, it needs to be reviewed and tagged as a "GPU Startup" subscription before GPU quota requests can succeed. If it's a non-Startups Azure Sponsorship offer, there's no self-service entitlement path at all.

#3 - No. The block applies to the GPU VM family category itself, not the size within it. `Standard_NC4as_T4_v3` at 4 vCPUs is already the smallest T4 configuration, so a smaller request won't get around it.

#4 - If you're on Microsoft for Startups Founders Hub credits, open a support ticket through the Founders Hub support portal, citing your Azure subscription ID and the quota request/operation ID, so the Startups team can review GPU eligibility and tagging.

results.title: 90 days, 5 support cases, zero answers: how Azure handles H100 capacity requests - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
In late June 2026 I opened quota requests for non-Spot H100 (ND/NC H100 v5) in five regions: UK South (2606280050000772), Australia East (2606240050000059), East US (2606280050000769), West Europe (2606280050000770), North Europe (2606280050000771).

...

- "All GPU SKUs are globally capacity constrained" (technical lead, case 2606240050000059), no ETA.
- Support cannot see or reach the capacity decision-makers (support engineer).
- "Severity B is the maximum for a backlogged request" - refusing Severity A on a total production outage.
- Two contradictory promised update dates, both missed.
- Eight different engineers rotating across the cases.

...

Hi Roee,

Azure quota and actual VM capacity are separate. An increased H100 quota does not guarantee that `ND/NC H100 v5` capacity is available in a region. Microsoft specifically notes that deployment can still fail when quota is available but regional capacity is constrained.

For your production case, keep the existing quota requests tied to the support cases and ask Azure Support to escalate them to the Compute capacity team. Microsoft’s quota guidance confirms that unfulfilled quota requests can be escalated through a support request.

Also note that the H100 SKUs are specialized GPU VM families: `Standard_ND96isr_H100_v5` provides 8 H100 GPUs, while `Standard_NC40ads_H100_v5` provides 1 H100 GPU.

Given the Spot evictions, include the production impact in the existing cases and request allocation for the specific regions/SKUs rather than submitting duplicate quota requests.

results.title: Storage Account V1 to V2 Migration - Impact on Function App Costs - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
The important distinction is that a Function App execution does not necessarily generate one Storage API transaction for every trigger. Azure Functions uses its associated storage account for runtime operations such as managing triggers, logging, scaling, and other internal state. The actual number of storage transactions depends on the Function App configuration and workload. Microsoft specifically notes that Event Hubs-triggered and Durable Functions workloads can generate a high volume of storage transactions. `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/storage-considerations`

Regarding the GPv1 → GPv2 migration:

- GPv1 has lower transaction prices, while GPv2 generally has lower capacity costs and provides additional features.
- Microsoft warns that workloads with high read/write/list activity can see higher transaction costs after moving to GPv2. `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-account-upgrade`
- Therefore, several thousand Function executions per day do not by themselves tell you the cost impact. You should measure the Storage transaction volume of the actual workload before migration.
- Microsoft provides a GPv1 → GPv2 Cost Estimator and recommends using the Azure Pricing Calculator to model the expected impact. `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/general-purpose-version-1-account-migration-frequently-asked-questions`
- https://github.com/microsoft/GPv1-Retirement-Cost-Estimator

...

Finally, GPv1 cannot be retained indefinitely. Microsoft is retiring GPv1 on October 13, 2026. Remaining GPv1 accounts will be automatically migrated to GPv2 if they haven't been upgraded, and the migration is permanent. `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/general-purpose-version-1-account-migration-overview`

So I would recommend:

1. Baseline the Storage transactions generated by each Function App.
2. Identify whether multiple Function Apps share the same storage account.
3. Estimate the GPv2 transaction cost using your actual usage.
4. Upgrade before October 13, 2026 rather than relying on automatic migration.

...

We have now completed a full analysis of our August 2026 billing data across all 11 GPv1 storage accounts in our subscription. The results confirm exactly what you described, but the scale of the impact is significant for us.

Our findings:

- Current monthly storage transaction cost across all GPv1 accounts: approximately £3.30
- Estimated monthly cost after GPv2 migration (Hot tier, LRS): approximately £357
- That is a ~108x increase, driven almost entirely by Azure Files Write Operations generated by the Azure Functions Consumption plan runtime (lease files, host state, trigger coordination)
- These Files Write operations account for 80-90% of the projected GPv2 cost despite being a small fraction of total transaction volume
- Our actual function workloads (IoT device APIs, alert processing, zone processing) are modest. The high transaction cost comes from the Consumption plan infrastructure overhead, not our application code.

We understand the migration is mandatory and that GPv1 cannot be retained past 13 October 2026. However, the correct fix for us is to migrate our Function Apps from the Consumption plan to either the Flex Consumption plan (which removes the Azure Files dependency) or a Dedicated App Service plan, before upgrading the storage accounts. This would eliminate the Files Write operations that are causing the cost increase.

results.title: Remain on Free Tier – Disable Automatic Upgrade to Pay-As-You-Go - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
According to the Azure OpenAI quota management documentation, `tierUpgradePolicy` controls whether a resource is automatically upgraded when a higher quota tier becomes available. Setting the policy to `NoAutoUpgrade` is the supported method to opt out of automatic tier upgrades.

The presence of:

- `nextTierName: Tier 1`
- `upgradeAvailabilityStatus: Available`

indicates that your resource is eligible for a Tier 1 upgrade, but these values alone do not indicate that the upgrade will be performed automatically.

If the `NoAutoUpgrade` policy is successfully applied and retained, the resource should remain on the Free Tier without being automatically upgraded to Tier 1. Converting a Free Trial subscription to Pay-As-You-Go is not required solely for opting out of automatic tier upgrades.
